seal.statement: Independent adversarial verification of the experimental raft-rs partition backend approved it with recorded defects and falsified none of the owner's five stop conditions, but it measured two that sit directly on the path the transport quest will take, and the owner has split them out as a prerequisite that must be independently approved before any real transport routing begins - because transport is precisely what introduces the caller paths that expose them, and proving transport first would leave its result ambiguous. The first is that the backend decides whether a failure was a WebAssembly fatal by asking whether the thrown value is an Error instance, while the boundary that asks encloses host JavaScript: every durable-store write in the Ready loop, the transport send hook, the address resolver that throws for a peer identity the local registry has not registered, and the application's own committed-entry callback. Measured twice by the verifier - closing a replica's SQLite handle retired the runtime and an unrelated group in it then refused dispatch, and a binding argument fault was called a fatal although no Rust ran - and reachable on the first real production write, which hands the core a JavaScript object where it needs bytes; the refusal branch of the repair this replaces has no test anywhere in the corpus. The second is that durable retirement gates the tick scheduler rather than the node, so a retired replica whose stale configuration still lists itself was driven directly through its own tick and raised the live cluster's term and cost it its leader, and admitted real envelopes besides; the property holds today only because the scheduler is the sole caller, which transport is about to stop being true. This quest fixes both and nothing else. It replaces the instance test with three structurally distinguished failure domains - a core refusal, which is a typed outcome of a normal raft-rs operation and never retires a runtime; a WebAssembly fatal, which is a trap or panic originating in the invocation itself or the binding's own explicit indication, and which marks its runtime unhealthy under the policy already recorded; and a host failure, which is JavaScript outside Rust and is neither of the others and carries its own recovery semantics - and it narrows the boundary that can classify a fatal to as close as practical around the invocation, so that persistence, sending, address resolution and application callbacks cannot be converted into a Raft-runtime fatal by throwing. Where the current surface leaves refusal and fatal ambiguous it changes the experimental binding minimally toward an unambiguous result rather than classifying exceptions more cleverly, and it resorts to matching a message only if the binding offers nothing stronger and a falsifier shows that adequate. It makes retirement an invariant of the node itself: a retired logical replica, after a restart and with no scheduler running, does not tick, campaign, accept inbound envelopes for active participation, originate traffic, accept proposals, or rejoin because stale local state still lists it, and the check happens before the core is touched rather than after, failing closed with a typed refusal. Retirement stays separate from the committed configuration, which continues to record what the node last knew about consensus membership while retirement records whether this local replica may participate at all, so retirement never rewrites the configuration and a retired identity is never reactivated by a later message. It does not resurrect the sender-membership rule an earlier evaluation falsified: for a replica that is not retired, inbound traffic still follows the corrected ingress semantics and a sender absent from the local applied configuration is still admitted. Its falsifiers are driven, not argued - each of the seven failure shapes the owner named, asserting the classification and whether the group, the runtime and unrelated groups remain usable; and the verifier's exact retirement reproducer, with the check then deliberately bypassed so the old disruptive behaviour reappears as a permanent load-bearing control. The apply-rollback invariant, outbound encoding, the committed-entry callback shape, the shared runtime singleton and the unregistered-peer workflow rule are recorded as inputs to the transport quest and are not absorbed here.

text: Lead ruling on the binding question phase 1 answered. MEASURED: the binding already makes a core refusal structurally distinguishable from a trap on the JavaScript side - jserr is JsValue::from_str and is the only Err constructor in the whole file, used 69 times with no other, so every refusal the binding can produce crosses as a string primitive and never as an Error, while a genuine raft-rs fatal arrives as a WebAssembly.RuntimeError. The owner's section 2 authorises exactly this: derive a structural discriminator from the binding, or change the binding to expose one. It is derivable, so we derive it and do NOT rebuild the wasm. The rule for phase 2 is therefore: a thrown string is a core refusal, a RuntimeError is a WASM fatal, anything else is a host failure - and after the boundary narrowing host JavaScript is outside the invocation in any case. This is not message-string matching, which the owner allowed only as a last resort: nothing depends on what a refusal says, only on what type it is. The implementer's caveat is accepted and its mitigation is required: the string tag is implicit, so one future js_sys::Error would silently reclassify a refusal as a host failure, and the receipt must therefore parse vendor/raft-rs-wasm/src/lib.rs and assert that every Err goes through jserr and that jserr is JsValue::from_str, so the discriminator is derived from the binding and breaks loudly rather than silently if the binding changes. The declared alternative - jserr returning a tagged object, one function changed and 69 call sites untouched - is recorded as available and cheap if the owner later wants the contract declared rather than derived; it costs a wasm rebuild with its thermal gate, digest and build-recipe updates, and is not taken now. The glue-thrown TypeError from proposing a non-byte value is left classifying as a host failure with no binding change, which is correct: it is neither the binding's Err nor a Rust trap. It is the shape the earlier verifier measured being called a fatal although no Rust ran, and receipt 6 drives it.

Three binding-level findings phase 1 recorded rather than absorbed (R17), all outside this quest's two boundaries and all inputs to the transport quest. ONE, and the most serious: proposing a JavaScript object does not throw - the generated glue reads its length as undefined and uint8_to_vec produces a zero-length command, so the core receives an EMPTY proposal. On a follower it surfaces as a dropped proposal, which is what the earlier verifier saw and reported as a misclassification, but on a leader it would commit an empty entry. partition-service-raft-write-commit.js:37 hands the provider exactly such an object, so this is the first real production write on this backend. This is worse than the misclassification it was found behind: it is silent acceptance of a malformed proposal rather than a refusal, and it belongs to the parked outbound-encoding item with that severity attached. TWO: a wrong-typed handle silently reaches another group, because the generated glue coerces the u32 argument and a string coerces to zero, so a caller passing a bad handle drives whatever group holds handle zero; negative and fractional handles are refused. THREE: a trap's measured blast radius is narrower than the recorded policy assumes - after the panic the trapping group's handle is gone from the binding's table, because the call had removed it and the abort skipped the re-insert, so that group answers invalid handle while the rest of the runtime still works and an unrelated create_node succeeds on the same instance. The recorded policy of retiring the whole runtime stands; the measured fact is that the trapped group's in-memory state is the part actually lost.
